explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Some of the scribes, the teachers of the law, and some Pharisees say, “Teacher, we want to see a sign from You.” They'd just watched Jesus heal a man, and they still came asking for a sign. I can't say why, because the text doesn't tell us.

I see why a blessing came to mind, since they do call Him Teacher. But the scribes and Pharisees ask for something else. They say, “Teacher, we want to see a sign from You.” A sign is the request, and no blessing is mentioned.

That one makes sense if you picture a quiet chat in a corner. But nothing in the text says they pull Jesus aside. They say to Him, “Teacher, we want to see a sign from You.” The ask is a sign, and it comes out in the open.

It sounds right, because Jesus' first words are heavy. But listen to how He finishes: “…none will be given it except the sign of the prophet Jonah.” That 'except' matters. So one sign is coming, and it's the sign of Jonah.

Yes, baker, you caught the 'except.' Jesus says, “…none will be given it except the sign of the prophet Jonah.” So this generation is not getting nothing. It gets one sign, and Jesus names it right there.

That's the one. Jesus says none will be given “except the sign of the prophet Jonah.” Jonah is the prophet we meet in the book that carries his name. He's the one Jesus points to in the very next verse.

Elijah, a prophet who spoke for the LORD in Israel (1 Kings 18:36), is a big name, so I get the pull. But Jesus doesn't mention him here. He says the sign is that of the prophet Jonah. I'd have to hold my mustache steady to tell you Elijah's name isn't in these verses, and it isn't.

Elisha was a prophet who followed Elijah (1 Kings 19:19-21), and I can see why he came to mind. Jesus doesn't name him in this passage, though. The sign He names is “the sign of the prophet Jonah.” Jonah is the answer.

That's right. Jesus says, “For as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish…” Three days, three nights, no rounding up. That number is the whole point of the comparison He's about to make.

Seven is a big number in the Bible, so I understand the guess. But Jesus says Jonah was in the belly of the great fish for “three days and three nights.” Three, baker. Seven doesn't show up in this verse at all.

Forty days and forty nights is a famous stretch of time. It's how long the rain fell in the flood in the days of Noah, who built the ark (Genesis 7:12). But for Jonah in the great fish, Jesus says three days and three nights. Different story, different number.

You've got it. Jesus says, “For as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so the Son of Man will be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth.” The 'as' and the 'so' line the two up. Same length of time for both.

I can see why you might hesitate, since one is a fish and the other is the heart of the earth. But Jesus lines them up on purpose. He says, “For as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so the Son of Man will be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth.” The time matches, so this one is true.

explanations.answer: They repented at the preaching of Jonah
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Jesus says the men of Nineveh will condemn this generation, “for they repented at the preaching of Jonah.” They heard the message and repented. Jesus sets that beside a generation that's asking for a sign.

explanations.answer: They gave Jonah great gifts of silver
explanations.explanation: Silver is a nice guess, but gifts aren't in this verse. Jesus gives the reason plainly: “for they repented at the preaching of Jonah.” Their repenting is what He points to. Jonah's pockets don't come into it.

explanations.answer: They sent Jonah back home in peace
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a warm way to end a visit, but it isn't what Jesus says. He gives the reason this way: “for they repented at the preaching of Jonah.” The men of Nineveh repented when they heard him. That's the reason in this verse.

Yes, greater. Jesus says, “…and now One greater than Jonah is here.” He's talking about Himself. Nineveh repented at Jonah's preaching, and One greater than Jonah is standing right in front of these people.

Wiser is close to the idea, and I like that you were thinking about wisdom. But Jesus' exact word is “greater.” He says, “…and now One greater than Jonah is here.” 'Wiser' only fits in the next verse, when He talks about Solomon's wisdom.
Bolder makes sense for a preacher walking into a city. But the word Jesus uses is “greater.” He says, “…and now One greater than Jonah is here.” No boldness contest in this verse.

That's the one. Jesus says the Queen of the South “came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon.” Solomon was David's son and a king of Israel, and people came from every nation to hear his wisdom (1 Kings 4:34). She made a long trip just to listen.

David, Israel's king (2 Samuel 5:3), is the right family, so I see where that came from. But Jesus says she came to hear “the wisdom of Solomon.” Solomon was David's son (2 Samuel 12:24). It was the son's wisdom she traveled for.

Hezekiah was a king of Judah (2 Kings 18:1-3), so you picked another king, and I respect that. But Jesus says she came from the ends of the earth “to hear the wisdom of Solomon.” Hezekiah isn't mentioned in this passage. Solomon is the one she came for.

I get it, because 'seeking rest' sounds like it should end with a nap. But Jesus says the unclean spirit “passes through arid places seeking rest and does not find it.” Notice the last part: does not find it. So this one is false.
Right, baker. Jesus says the unclean spirit “passes through arid places seeking rest and does not find it.” It goes looking and comes up empty. That's what sets up the spirit's next move.

That's right. Jesus says the spirit finds the house “vacant, swept clean, and put in order.” Nobody's home, and everything's tidy. I've seen a spotless counter in my day, and it didn't mean anyone was cooking.
Locked and boarded up would be a very different picture. Jesus says the spirit finds the house “vacant, swept clean, and put in order.” Nothing about locks or boards. The way back in is open.
That would be a rough day for the house. But Jesus says the spirit finds it “vacant, swept clean, and put in order.” The house is still standing, tidy and empty. No smoke, no ashes.
Seven is right. Jesus says the spirit “brings with it seven other spirits more wicked than itself.” That's seven more, and each one is more wicked than the first spirit. They all go in together.

Yes, worse. Jesus says, “And the final plight of that man is worse than the first.” The man ends up in a harder spot than where he began. Jesus then says this is how it will be with this wicked generation.

Three is a number we heard earlier, with Jonah's days and nights, so it's easy to carry over. But for the spirits, Jesus says seven. The spirit “brings with it seven other spirits more wicked than itself.” Three belongs to the fish and the heart of the earth.

I understand wanting a happy ending, baker, but Jesus doesn't give one here. He says, “And the final plight of that man is worse than the first.” Worse is the word, not better. The last state is harder than the first.

Twelve is a big number, but it's not the one in this verse. Jesus says the spirit “brings with it seven other spirits more wicked than itself.” The number is seven. Count them again and you'll land on the same thing.

That's right, baker. After the picture of the spirit and the house, Jesus says, “So will it be with this wicked generation.” He's tying the picture back to the people in front of Him. That's where the whole picture was heading.

The men of Nineveh did come up earlier, so I see why they stuck. But Jesus used them as people who repented at Jonah's preaching. For the spirit and the house, He says, “So will it be with this wicked generation.” Nineveh isn't the one in this picture.

Solomon was in the passage a few verses back, so he's fresh in your mind. But the spirit's house isn't called his, and Jesus never says it is. He ends the picture with, “So will it be with this wicked generation.” That's who He's talking about.
That's right. Someone tells Jesus His mother and brothers are outside, and He answers, “Who is My mother, and who are My brothers?” Two questions in one breath. He doesn't just say yes or no.
I can see it feeling like a plain reply, since the message was plain. But Jesus does answer with a question. He says, “Who is My mother, and who are My brothers?” So this one is true.
Right, baker. The text says, “Pointing to His disciples, He said, ‘Here are My mother and My brothers.’” Disciples are the people who follow Jesus. He points right at them as He says it.

The scribes were the ones asking for a sign back at the start of this passage, so they're easy to remember. But in this moment, the text says Jesus was “Pointing to His disciples.” His disciples are the ones He calls His mother and brothers.

Neighbors is a friendly guess, and I'm all for friendly. But the text says Jesus was “Pointing to His disciples.” That's the group He points at when He says, “Here are My mother and My brothers.” No neighbors are mentioned.

explanations.answer: Whoever does the will of His Father
explanations.explanation: That's it. Jesus says, “For whoever does the will of My Father in heaven is My brother and sister and mother.” He's talking about doing the will of His Father in heaven. Whoever does that is family to Him.

explanations.answer: Whoever was born into His family
explanations.explanation: Birth is a natural thing to think of, since His mother and brothers had just been mentioned. But the text says nothing here about being born into His family as the test. Jesus says, “For whoever does the will of My Father in heaven is My brother and sister and mother.” That's the answer He gives.

explanations.answer: Whoever lives in His own hometown
explanations.explanation: I can see the logic, since neighbors can feel like family. But Jesus never mentions a hometown in this passage. He says, “For whoever does the will of My Father in heaven is My brother and sister and mother.” It's about doing the will of His Father.
